title: Disability & Umbrella Coverage
description: The paycheck if you cannot work, and extra liability if a lawsuit runs past the limit.
wolfLine: Insure the income. Then look at what a lawsuit could reach.

waiting-period.definition: The time between becoming disabled and the day a disability policy starts paying. Also called the elimination period.
waiting-period.example: A 90-day waiting period means about three months with no benefit, so savings or sick pay have to cover it.

disability-insurance.definition: Insurance that replaces part of your income if an illness or injury keeps you from working.
disability-insurance.example: You earn $5,000 a month. A policy that pays 60% would pay $3,000 a month while you qualify.

umbrella-policy.definition: Extra liability coverage that sits on top of your auto or home liability limits when a lawsuit blows past them.
umbrella-policy.example: Auto liability stops at $250,000. A lawsuit is $900,000. An umbrella can cover the $650,000 gap, up to its own limit.

lessons.title: Income Insurance
lessons.summary: Your paycheck is the asset. This policy protects it.

steps.context: [[Disability insurance]] is income insurance. Work sometimes offers a short version. It is not the same as life insurance, which pays after you die.
steps.prompt: What does disability insurance replace?
choices: Part of your income if you cannot work
Your medical bills
A life insurance death benefit
steps.explain: The loss is the paycheck that stops.

steps.prompt: If you do not work, disability insurance has a paycheck to replace.
steps.explain: No earned income, nothing for this policy to replace.

steps.prompt: Why do people skip this and then regret it?
choices: A long illness is more common than they think, and the paycheck stops anyway
The premium is higher than the benefit
Most policies stop paying after a week
steps.explain: The premium looks optional until the paychecks stop.

steps.prompt: You earn $4,000 a month. You miss three months of work with no disability coverage and no paid leave. How much pay is missing?
Disability insurance protects your ___.
choices: income
medical bills
savings
steps.explain: The bills stay. The paycheck is what this policy stands in for.

lessons.title: Short Term and Long Term
lessons.summary: One covers weeks. The other covers the year you did not plan.

steps.context: Short-term coverage often runs for a few months. Long-term coverage can run for years. A job’s plan may offer one, both, or neither.
steps.prompt: Short-term disability is built for:
choices: A few weeks or months away from work
Several years of illness
Only injuries at work
steps.explain: It is the bridge. It is not the whole road.

steps.prompt: Long-term disability is built for:
choices: An illness or injury that keeps you out for a long stretch
A few days off with the flu
A one-week recovery from minor surgery
steps.explain: That is the policy that matters if you cannot return this year.

steps.prompt: Short-term coverage makes long-term coverage unnecessary.
steps.explain: The short policy ends. The long one is what is left.

steps.prompt: Your job offers short-term disability at 60% of pay for 12 weeks, and nothing after. What is the hole?
choices: Any illness that lasts longer than those 12 weeks
Any illness that starts on a weekend
Doctor visits during those 12 weeks
steps.explain: Week 13 is the hole.

steps.prompt: Short-term pays $600 a week for 12 weeks. What is the most it will pay?

lessons.title: How Much It Pays
lessons.summary: It replaces a percent, not the whole paycheck.

steps.context: Read the percent and whose definition of disability the policy uses. Some pay only if you cannot do any job. Others pay if you cannot do your own.
steps.prompt: You earn $5,000 a month. The policy pays 60%. What is the monthly benefit?
What is that benefit for a year?
Your old pay for a year was $60,000. How much pay is not replaced?
A 60% policy pays your full salary.
steps.explain: Sixty percent is sixty percent. The other forty still has to come from somewhere.

steps.prompt: Why might a policy that covers “your own job” pay when a stricter one would not?
choices: You cannot do your work, even if you could do some other work
It pays a higher percent of your salary
It has no waiting period
steps.explain: The definition of disability is the gate. Read it.

lessons.title: The Benefit Summary
lessons.summary: Percent, waiting period, and the job test.

steps.context: The [[waiting period]] is 90 days. The policy pays nothing during the wait.
steps.prompt: What is the monthly benefit on this page?
steps.explain: That line says $3,000.

steps.prompt: The premium is $45 a month. What is that per year?
You are hurt on day 1. When does this summary say benefits can start?
choices: After the 90-day waiting period
The same week
When your sick days run out, whatever the policy says
steps.explain: The wait is part of the price. Savings have to cover it.

steps.prompt: “Your own occupation” means the policy only pays if every job on earth is impossible.
steps.explain: It means your own job. A stricter policy says any job.

steps.prompt: Three months of waiting, and your pay is $5,000 a month. How much pay is missing before benefits start, if you have no other leave?

lessons.title: Umbrella Coverage
lessons.summary: When a lawsuit is taller than the policy underneath.

steps.context: An [[umbrella policy]] needs enough [[liability coverage|liability-coverage]] underneath it. Insurers usually require that floor.
steps.prompt: What is an umbrella policy?
choices: Extra liability coverage above your auto or home limits
A policy that replaces your auto and home liability
Coverage for damage to your own car and home
steps.explain: It starts where the other liability limit stops.

steps.prompt: Auto liability stops at $250,000. The lawsuit is $900,000. How much is above the auto limit?
Who looks at an umbrella?
choices: Someone whose savings or home could be reached by a large lawsuit
Someone whose car already has high collision coverage
Someone with no car, no home, and no savings
steps.explain: The umbrella protects what a judgment could take.

steps.prompt: An umbrella replaces the need for any auto liability coverage.
steps.explain: It sits on top. The insurer will ask for a solid policy underneath.

steps.prompt: In this example the umbrella premium is $300 a year. Over 10 years, what is that premium?
steps.explain: $300 × 10 = $3,000. A real quote can differ. The shape is a small premium under a large limit.

lessons.title: An Insurance Checklist
lessons.summary: Name the hole before the year names it for you.

steps.prompt: Solid enough for now, or worth a look?
items: Health plan in force, and you know the deductible
Renters or home policy, and you know if flood is excluded
Auto liability at the state minimum only
No disability coverage, and you live on your paycheck
Life insurance through work equal to one year of pay, with a new baby at home
steps.explain: A minimum, a missing income policy, and a thin life benefit are the looks. A plan you understand can sit.

steps.prompt: Why is “auto liability at the state minimum only” worth a look?
choices: The legal floor is often too small for a serious injury
State minimums are the maximum the law allows
Minimum policies have higher deductibles
steps.explain: Legal and enough are still different words.

steps.prompt: A checklist replaces reading the policy.
steps.explain: The checklist tells you which policy to open.

steps.prompt: You rent, and you have no renters policy. Where does that land?
choices: Worth a look. The landlord’s policy is not yours
Solid. Renters are covered by the building
Solid, if the landlord has good insurance
steps.explain: Your belongings and your liability are uninsured until you buy the policy.

steps.prompt: The point of the list is to find the ___ before a loss does.
choices: hole
cheapest premium
biggest policy
steps.explain: A named hole can be priced. A surprise cannot.

lessons.title: Putting It Together
lessons.summary: Look for the hole, not the matching premium.

steps.context: Same health premium. The rest of the sketch is the decision.

docs.title: Sketch A
docs.subtitle: Health, and a thin auto limit

steps.prompt: Both sketches pay $1,080 a year for health insurance. What is Sketch A missing that Sketch B has?
choices: A higher auto liability limit and a disability benefit
A cheaper health premium
A lower deductible
steps.explain: The health line matches. The protection does not.

docs.title: Sketch A
docs.subtitle: Health, and a thin auto limit

steps.prompt: How much higher is Sketch B’s auto liability limit than Sketch A’s $25,000?
You live on your paycheck and Sketch A has no disability benefit. What is the exposed piece?
choices: Your income if you cannot work
The health premium, which is unpaid
A death benefit
steps.explain: The health plan pays doctors. It does not replace the paycheck.

steps.prompt: Matching health premiums means the two sketches protect you equally.
steps.explain: The auto limit and the disability line are the difference.

steps.prompt: Which sketch is the sturdier starting point?
choices: Sketch B
Sketch A
They are the same stack
why: A’s $25,000 limit is the thin one.
The health premiums match. The rest does not.
steps.explain: B raised the liability ceiling and insured the paycheck.

lessons.title: Elena’s Yearly Review
lessons.summary: A raise is a reason to reread the stack.

story.title: The afternoon she reads the stack
story.body:
Once a year, after her raise, Elena reads the stack. She earns **$60,000**. Her long-term disability policy would pay **60%**, which is **$36,000** a year, or **$3,000** a month, after a **90**-day wait.

Her auto liability limit is **$100,000**. She owns a small condo and has **$40,000** in savings. A serious crash could reach past that limit. She prices an umbrella and writes the date of this review on the folder.

steps.prompt: What is 60% of Elena’s $60,000 salary?
What is that benefit per month?
The waiting period is 90 days. About how many months is that?
steps.explain: 90 ÷ 30 = 3 months. She needs savings for the wait.

steps.prompt: Why is a $100,000 auto limit worth a look, given the condo and the savings?
choices: A lawsuit could reach past $100,000 and into what she owns
Condo insurance cancels auto liability
Savings make liability unnecessary
steps.explain: The limit is the ceiling on the insurer. Her condo sits above it.

steps.prompt: She can skip the review next year because she did it once.
steps.explain: A raise, a baby, a move, or a new car changes the stack.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Disability & Umbrella
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Pay is $3,000 a month. Disability pays 50%. What is the monthly benefit?
An umbrella policy sits where?
choices: Above the liability limits you already have
Instead of health insurance
Inside a term life premium
steps.explain: It is extra liability coverage, not a replacement for the policy under it.

steps.prompt: Short-term disability that ends at 12 weeks covers a two-year illness.
steps.explain: The short policy ends. The rest needs long-term coverage or savings.

steps.prompt: Which gap deserves a look this year?
choices: No income coverage, and your paycheck pays the rent
A health plan whose deductible you already know
A renters policy you reread in January
steps.explain: The missing paycheck is the hole. A plan you understand is not.
